narrative:
The decision to deny your application is based on a model that estimates your chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. That probability came out to 52.5%, meaning you are more likely to fail than to pass. This is not an overwhelming margin, but it was enough to tilt the decision against you.

The single most important factor in this estimate was your LSAT score. At 32, it is roughly five points below the average of accepted applicants. This was by far the strongest influence, and it pushed squarely in the direction of failing the exam. Because no other factor was strong enough to counteract it, your overall risk stayed above the critical threshold for admission.

Interestingly, the next two most important factors actually worked in your favor. Your undergraduate GPA, although lower than the typical admitted student's 3.23, was interpreted as a modest point in your favor, nudging the risk downward. Likewise, your third-year class standing was below the average of admitted students, yet it also pushed your predicted risk slightly toward passing. These favorable nudges existed, but they were much weaker than the negative pull of the LSAT. In short, the model recognized some underlying ability and a slightly positive trajectory, but it could not compensate for a test score it considers the strongest predictor of first-try bar success.

Your next move is clear: focus on raising your LSAT score. With a stronger score, the overall balance of evidence would shift considerably in your direction. Consider retaking the exam after additional preparation and then reapplying. Improving your test performance could move your profile from rejection to ready.
